text:
An AI agent is a software system in which a language model participates in a loop involving decisions, tools, observations, and further actions. A simple LLM call maps an input to an output, while an agent can decide what action should happen next.

Agentic workflows can contain deterministic steps such as prompt chaining, routing, and parallel execution. More autonomous agents can select tools and determine their next actions based on intermediate results.

Tool calling allows a model to request a specific software function. Tools might include search, database access, filesystem operations, code execution, APIs, or project-management systems. The application should validate tool arguments and enforce permissions rather than allowing arbitrary operations.

An orchestrator-worker architecture uses one component to decompose a task and other components to perform specialized subtasks. An evaluator-optimizer pattern uses one model or process to critique an output and another iteration to improve it.

Agentic RAG combines retrieval with iterative reasoning. An agent may decide that it needs project documentation, retrieve relevant information, inspect the result, and then perform another retrieval with a refined query.

Memory can be divided into short-term conversation state and longer-lived information. Long-term memory should be selective and structured rather than blindly storing every conversation.

text:
Agents introduce additional failure modes. They can select inappropriate tools, enter loops, make incorrect assumptions, or spend excessive computation. Production agents therefore need limits on iterations, tool permissions, time, and resource usage.

For software engineering assistants, useful agent tasks include repository investigation, test failure analysis, documentation lookup, code review, and controlled project modifications.

text:
BM25 is a lexical information retrieval ranking function based on term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization. It is widely used in search engines and information retrieval systems.

The intuition behind BM25 is straightforward. A term that occurs in a query and appears frequently in a particular document contributes evidence that the document is relevant. A term appearing in many documents is less discriminative and therefore contributes less. Document length is also considered so that very long documents do not receive an unfair advantage simply because they contain more terms.

text:
BM25 tokenization is an important practical consideration. A simple implementation may lowercase text and split on whitespace. Production systems often use more sophisticated tokenization, stemming, stop-word handling, punctuation processing, or language-specific analyzers.

BM25 is particularly useful for exact technical terminology. A query containing OAuth2, Eureka, PersistentClient, HTTP 429, or NullPointerException can benefit from lexical matching because the exact token can be highly informative.

BM25 does not understand meaning in the same way as an embedding model. A passage can be conceptually relevant while sharing few words with the query, and BM25 may rank it poorly. Dense retrieval provides complementary semantic matching.

text:
The rank-bm25 Python package provides a simple BM25 implementation. It can be used to build an in-memory index from tokenized documents and obtain a score for every document for a query. The highest scoring document indexes can then be returned.

For a production system, the BM25 index should not be rebuilt for every query. Index construction should be a separate ingestion step. The resulting index should be persisted or maintained by a dedicated search engine when the dataset becomes large.

BM25 is therefore best viewed as one component of a retrieval architecture rather than a replacement for semantic search.

Docker packages applications and their dependencies into containers. A container image is a portable artifact containing an application, runtime, libraries, and filesystem content required to run the application.

A Dockerfile describes how an image is built. Common instructions include FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE, and CMD or ENTRYPOINT. Multi-stage builds can separate compilation dependencies from the smaller runtime image.

Containers are created from images. A container has an isolated process environment and can communicate with other containers through Docker networking.

Port mapping exposes a container port through the host. For example, mapping host port 8080 to container port 80 allows a web server inside the container to be accessed through the host.

Docker image layers affect build performance and storage. Placing stable dependency installation steps before frequently changing source files can improve build caching.

Embeddings are numerical vectors that represent information in a continuous space. In natural language applications, an embedding model converts text into a vector containing many floating-point values. Texts with related meanings can produce vectors that are close under a similarity metric.

Embedding models are different from generative language models. A generative model such as Llama can produce text, while an embedding model is optimized to represent input information for comparison, clustering, or retrieval.

A typical semantic search pipeline embeds every document chunk during indexing. When a user submits a query, the same embedding model is used to embed the query. The retrieval system compares the query vector with stored vectors and returns the nearest candidates.

Using the same embedding model for documents and queries is important because the vectors need to live in a compatible representation space. Changing the embedding model usually requires re-indexing the collection.

Chunk representation affects embedding quality. A chunk with insufficient context may produce an ambiguous representation. A contextual retrieval approach can prepend or associate a concise description of where the chunk belongs in the document before generating its embedding. The original chunk can still be preserved separately for generation.

Embedding dimensions, normalization, distance metrics, model domain, and language coverage can affect retrieval performance. A model that performs well on general text may behave differently on source code, API documentation, scientific papers, or highly specialized terminology.

Embedding retrieval is semantic rather than exact. A query about storing vectors may retrieve a passage describing vector databases even when the query and passage do not share many exact words. However, semantic retrieval can sometimes miss exact identifiers or terminology. Hybrid retrieval addresses this by combining embeddings with lexical search.

text:
Hybrid search combines multiple retrieval strategies so that the strengths of one method can compensate for weaknesses in another. In technical knowledge systems, a common combination is dense semantic retrieval and lexical retrieval using BM25.

Dense retrieval converts a query into an embedding and finds semantically similar chunks. It is effective when the query uses different wording from the source. For example, a question about giving an LLM external knowledge may retrieve passages describing grounded generation even if the phrase external knowledge does not occur.

text:
Lexical retrieval operates on words and term frequencies. BM25 is a popular ranking function for keyword search. It rewards terms that occur in a document while accounting for document length and the fact that common words are less informative.

Dense and lexical scores are not normally directly comparable. A vector similarity score and a BM25 score have different scales and meanings. A common way to combine their rankings is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

RRF uses the rank position assigned by each retriever rather than directly adding raw scores. A simplified formula is RRF(d) = sum over retrievers of 1 divided by k plus rank(d), where k is a smoothing constant often set to 60.

text:
For example, if a chunk is ranked second by dense retrieval and first by BM25, its fused score is 1/(60+2) + 1/(60+1). A chunk appearing near the top in both retrieval lists receives contributions from both systems.

A practical hybrid pipeline retrieves a candidate pool from each retriever, often larger than the final number of results. For example, dense retrieval may return 20 candidates and BM25 may return 20 candidates. RRF merges those candidates and produces a smaller final set such as five chunks.

Candidate depth matters. If each retriever returns only three candidates, a relevant document ranked fourth by both systems cannot reach the fusion stage. Increasing the candidate pool gives fusion more evidence but increases computation.

Large language model inference is the process of using a trained model to produce outputs for an input prompt. The input may contain system instructions, user messages, retrieved documents, tool results, and conversation history.

Inference begins with tokenization. Text is converted into tokens that the model processes. The model predicts a probability distribution over possible next tokens. A decoding strategy then selects tokens until a stopping condition is reached.

Temperature controls the randomness of token selection by modifying the distribution before sampling. Lower temperatures generally produce more deterministic outputs, while higher temperatures allow more variation. Deterministic settings are often useful for retrieval evaluation and structured engineering tasks.

text:
Context length limits how much information can be supplied to a model in a single request. A RAG system therefore has to select useful evidence rather than blindly inserting an entire corpus into the prompt.

Local inference can be performed using tools such as Ollama. Running a model locally can reduce dependency on external APIs and can be useful for privacy-sensitive development. The tradeoffs include memory requirements, model size, inference speed, and hardware limitations.

Quantization reduces the precision used to represent model weights and can lower memory requirements. Common approaches include 8-bit and 4-bit quantization. Quantization can make local models practical on consumer hardware, although quality and speed can vary.

text:
Microservices architecture decomposes an application into independently deployable services organized around business capabilities. Each service owns a focused responsibility and communicates with other services through APIs or messaging.

Service boundaries should reflect meaningful domain responsibilities rather than simply splitting a monolith into many small applications. Excessive fragmentation can create network overhead, operational complexity, distributed transactions, and difficult debugging.

Synchronous communication is commonly implemented with HTTP or gRPC. Asynchronous communication can use message brokers such as RabbitMQ or Kafka. Messaging can decouple producers and consumers and is useful when work does not need to complete within the original request.

Service discovery allows services to find one another without hardcoding every network location. A registry can maintain information about available service instances. Load balancing distributes requests across instances.

Configuration management separates environment-specific settings from application code. Secrets should be stored securely rather than committed to source control.

Observability is essential in distributed systems. Logs, metrics, traces, correlation IDs, and health checks help engineers understand requests that cross service boundaries.

Authentication and authorization should be designed consistently. OAuth2 and OpenID Connect are common standards for identity and delegated access. A gateway can enforce some cross-cutting policies, but services should still validate security-sensitive information where appropriate.

Distributed systems require careful handling of retries, timeouts, idempotency, circuit breaking, and partial failures. A service that waits indefinitely for another service can exhaust resources and cause cascading failures.

Containers are commonly used to package microservices. Docker Compose can provide a convenient local environment containing multiple services and infrastructure dependencies such as PostgreSQL, Redis, and RabbitMQ.

Prompt engineering is the practice of designing the input supplied to a language model so that the model performs a desired task reliably. In an engineering system, prompts should be treated as part of the application rather than casual text.

A useful prompt often separates system instructions, task requirements, context, and the user request. Explicit boundaries help prevent retrieved text from being confused with instructions.

In RAG applications, retrieved documents should be clearly identified as evidence. The model can be instructed to answer using the supplied evidence and to acknowledge when the evidence does not contain enough information.

Structured output is useful when the result must be consumed by software. A system can specify a JSON schema or use a typed model such as Pydantic to validate fields. This is more reliable than asking a model to produce arbitrary prose and attempting to parse it afterward.

Few-shot examples can demonstrate the desired input-output format. However, examples consume context and should be used when they provide measurable value.

Prompt injection is a security concern when untrusted documents or user content are placed into an LLM context. Retrieved content may contain text that looks like instructions. Applications should distinguish data from control instructions and avoid granting models unnecessary authority.

Chunking is important because documents are normally too large to retrieve or pass to a model as a single unit. Fixed-size chunking is simple, while recursive or semantic chunking attempts to preserve meaningful boundaries. Metadata such as source name, page number, section, or document identifier can be retained so that the final response can provide citations.

text:
RAG does not automatically guarantee factual answers. Retrieval quality, chunk quality, prompt construction, model behavior, and evaluation all affect the result. A system can hallucinate even when retrieval succeeds if the model ignores evidence or if the retrieved evidence is insufficient.

Advanced RAG systems can use contextual retrieval, hybrid search, query rewriting, reranking, multi-stage retrieval, caching, and retrieval evaluation. Contextual retrieval adds document-level information to individual chunks before embedding them. Hybrid retrieval combines lexical retrieval such as BM25 with dense semantic retrieval. Reranking applies a second relevance model to a candidate set before generation.

Redis is an in-memory data store commonly used for caching, counters, distributed coordination, queues, and other low-latency workloads. Data is stored in memory, which makes many operations fast.

Caching can reduce database load and application latency. A cache-aside strategy commonly checks Redis first. If the value is absent, the application reads from the primary database and then stores the result in Redis.

Cache invalidation is a major design concern. Cached data can become stale when the source of truth changes. TTL values provide automatic expiration, while explicit invalidation can remove or update keys after writes.

Redis supports several data structures including strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, and streams. The appropriate structure depends on the access pattern.

text:
Distributed locks can coordinate work across application instances, but they must be designed carefully. Lock expiration, ownership, retries, and failure scenarios all matter.

Redis can also be used for rate limiting. A service can maintain counters associated with users or API keys and reject requests after a configured threshold.

Pub/sub provides a lightweight messaging mechanism, while Redis Streams provide a more durable event-oriented structure with consumer groups.

Persistence options allow Redis data to survive process restarts, but Redis should not automatically be treated as a replacement for a durable relational database. The correct durability configuration depends on the workload.

Reranking is a second-stage retrieval technique used to improve the ordering of an initial candidate set. Instead of asking an expensive relevance model to score an entire corpus, a fast retriever first produces a manageable set of candidates and a stronger model then evaluates those candidates more carefully.

A typical retrieval pipeline can contain three stages: candidate generation, reranking, and answer generation. Candidate generation may use dense vector search, BM25, or hybrid retrieval. Reranking receives the query and each candidate passage and estimates how relevant that passage is to the query.

Cross-encoder rerankers are one common approach. Unlike bi-encoder embedding models that independently encode the query and document, a cross-encoder processes the query and candidate together. This allows detailed token-level interactions but is more computationally expensive.

Reranking is useful when the first-stage retrieval returns several plausible candidates but their ordering is imperfect. For example, hybrid search may retrieve ten candidates containing useful information. A reranker can reorder those candidates so that the passages most directly answering the question appear first.

The candidate pool should be larger than the final context size. A system might retrieve 20 or 50 candidates and rerank them before selecting the top 5. The appropriate values depend on latency, model size, and corpus size.

Reranking introduces latency and computational cost. It should therefore be applied after inexpensive retrieval rather than to the entire document collection.

Reranking quality should be evaluated separately from candidate generation. If the relevant document never enters the candidate pool, a reranker cannot recover it. This is why recall at the candidate-generation stage is an important metric.

System design is the process of deciding how software components interact to satisfy functional and non-functional requirements. A design should begin with requirements rather than technology choices.

Functional requirements describe what the system must do. Non-functional requirements describe properties such as availability, latency, throughput, durability, consistency, security, and scalability.

A typical design exercise starts by estimating traffic and data volume. Requests per second, peak traffic, storage growth, object sizes, and read/write ratios influence architecture decisions.

Load balancing distributes traffic across multiple application instances. Horizontal scaling adds instances rather than relying on a single increasingly powerful machine.

text:
The Transformer architecture was introduced by Vaswani and colleagues in 2017 and became the foundation for many modern language models. Transformers replaced recurrence with attention mechanisms that allow tokens to interact directly.

Self-attention computes relationships between tokens using query, key, and value representations. Given matrices Q, K, and V, scaled dot-product attention is commonly expressed as softmax(QK transpose divided by the square root of the key dimension) multiplied by V.

Multi-head attention allows the model to learn different types of relationships in parallel. Each attention head can focus on different aspects of the input. The outputs of the heads are combined and passed through additional transformations.

A vector database stores numerical representations of information called embeddings and provides similarity search over those vectors. Embeddings allow text, images, or other data to be represented in a continuous vector space where related concepts can have nearby representations.

Traditional relational databases are optimized for structured queries involving exact values, joins, indexes, and predicates. Common similarity measures include cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, and dot product.
